<explanation>
Below is a tailored guide for drawing an accurate system design diagram for the “Circle” project—an issue-and-project management interface built with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui. Use this as a blueprint to capture every major architectural element and their interactions.

1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   • This is a full-stack (primarily frontend) web application built on Next.js.  
   • It provides a modern, responsive UI for tracking issues, projects, teams, and members.  
   • Currently it uses in-memory/mock data; no external backend services are integrated yet.

2. Main components to include  
   a. Client Browser  
      - Renders the app, issues HTTP requests, executes client-side React code after hydration.  
   b. Next.js Server Runtime  
      - Handles file-based routing, server-side rendering (SSR), static generation (SSG), and serves assets.  
      - Entry points: `/app` directory pages (e.g., `app/page.tsx`, `app/[orgId]/…`).  
   c. React Pages & Layout  
      - Pages folder: domain routes for organizations, projects, issues, teams, settings.  
      - `components/layout`: global layout, sidebar, headers, theme provider.  
   d. UI Component Library  
      - `components/ui`: primitive UI building blocks (buttons, dialogs, tables, etc.) from shadcn/ui + Tailwind.  
      - `components/common`: domain-specific components (issues grid, project badges, member lists, etc.).  
   e. State Management Layer  
      - `store/*-store.ts`: Zustand or similar stores (issuesStore, filterStore, createIssueStore, viewStore, searchStore).  
      - Provides a single source of truth for client-side state, supports both SSR hydration & client updates.  
   f. Data Layer  
      - `mock-data/*.ts(x)`: static JSON/TS modules that simulate API responses (issues, projects, teams, users).  
      - `lib/utils.ts`: helper functions for data manipulation (e.g., date formatting).  
   g. Static Assets  
      - `public/images`: icons, logos.  
      - Global CSS: `app/globals.css`, Tailwind config in `postcss.config.mjs`.

3. Relationships and data flows  
   • User initiates HTTP(S) request → Next.js Server → selects matching page in `/app` → executes its `getServerSideProps` or uses SSG → fetches mock-data via stores or custom hooks → renders React to HTML → sends to client.  
   • On hydration, client-side React takes over: pages/components call stores/hooks → read/write state → update UI.  
   • UI components dispatch actions to stores → stores read/write mock-data (in real-world this layer stands in for API calls).

4. Architectural patterns & design principles  
   • File-based routing (Next.js App Router) for domain pages.  
   • Separation of concerns:  
     – Layout vs. feature pages vs. UI primitives vs. domain components.  
     – Centralized client state (Zustand stores) separate from UI logic.  
   • Atomic design in UI library: primitives → composed common components → pages.  
   • Mock-data layer easily switchable to real API integration in future.

5. Diagramming guidelines  
   a. Use distinct shapes/colors:  
      – Client Browser (browser icon, blue)  
      – Next.js Server (server box, green)  
      – Component Layer (stack of boxes, orange)  
      – State Stores (cylinder or database icon, purple)  
      – Mock-Data (stack of files icon, gray)  
   b. Label each component clearly: e.g., “app/layout.tsx”, “issues-store”, “mock-data/issues.ts”  
   c. Draw directional arrows to show:  
      – Browser → Next.js Server (HTTP request)  
      – Server → File-based Router → Page Component  
      – Component → Store → Mock-Data  
      – Store → Component (state updates)  
   d. Group related items inside containers:  
      – “/app” folder as one box containing pages and layout  
      – “/components” folder divided into “ui primitives” and “domain components”  
      – “/store” folder as the state management cluster  
   e. Annotate interactions: SSR vs. CSR, hydration boundary.

6. Tailoring the diagram to this project  
   • Emphasize Next.js App Router: show nested layout (`layout.tsx`), dynamic route segments (`[orgId]`, `[teamId]`).  
   • Highlight shadcn/ui and Tailwind CSS in the UI primitives layer.  
   • Show where global theming (`theme-provider.tsx`) lives.  
   • Depict how mock-data modules feed into stores—plan to swap these out for real APIs.  
   • Indicate future extension points: API routes (`/pages/api`), database layer.

7. Final checklist for the diagram  
   – [ ] Clear labels on every component, folder, and file group.  
   – [ ] Directional arrows for all data flows (requests, state changes).  
   – [ ] Color coding or distinct shapes per layer (client, server, components, state, data).  
   – [ ] Grouping containers matching the on-disk directory structure.  
   – [ ] Notes on SSR vs. CSR boundaries and hydrations.

By following this guide, you’ll produce a comprehensive system design diagram that mirrors the “Circle” codebase structure, highlights key architectural patterns, and clearly communicates data flows and extension points. Keep the diagram up to date as the project evolves—especially when replacing mock-data with real API services or adding serverless functions.  
</explanation>
